title: What the guarded media fetch refuses, and under which code
pins: Which URLs `fetchPublicUrlContent()` refuses, and under WHICH CODE, in every language. The code is the contract â€” a consumer switches on it to decide whether to widen an allow-list, surface a hard stop, or report an SSRF attempt. The message is deliberately not pinned: the three implementations word these differently on purpose, and a test over the prose holds every language to a translation and reddens on a wording improvement that changed nothing. Same decision as `browser-url-policy`, and the same spellings â€” `private_address_refused` is one finding with one name across the ecosystem.
scope: The refusal decision and stable code of the opt-in guarded media fetch. PHP and TypeScript retain their pre-existing unguarded fetch methods, exercised by url-0009; Python has no unguarded fetch method by design. This suite does not establish byte handling or complete SSRF protection: a name can resolve differently between the check and the request, which only connection-level pinning closes.
findings: Writing this corpus exposed the need for machine-readable refusal codes; the PHP reference gained them in prism 07f842b. The TypeScript and Python guards now reproduce the ten recorded refusal outcomes and the successful public-fetch control. This establishes agreement for those inputs, with initial refusals sending no request and the refused redirect target never requested; it does not establish that every URL is safe or that an identical defect cannot exist in all three implementations. PHP and TypeScript alone exercise url-0009: Python explicitly skips the legacy unguarded-path control because that API never existed there, so agrees remains false on that row. DNS rebinding between validation and connection remains unclosed in all three guards. All five refusal codes are now compared in the common corpus. url-0012 repeats a public self-redirect in every fake response and records too_many_redirects from all three runners; its six-request assertion pins the default allowance at five redirect hops in every language. Each behavioral suite also retains a successful chain within the bound as a discrimination control (G-71). G-89 (2026-10-17): url-0013..0016 add the spellings ALL THREE guards admitted while agreeing on every earlier row -- Alibaba Cloud's metadata endpoint in CGNAT, and the NAT64 and 6to4 spellings of 169.254.169.254, as literals and as a DNS answer. A corpus comparing languages cannot see a defect they share; these rows were found by asking what a hostile address does, not by comparison. url-0017 is the control that NAT64 of a public address still fetches, so refusing NAT64 outright fails. Corpus 0.1.29 adds url-0018 to url-0023 (G-366): ISATAP addresses behind a public 6to4 prefix, as literals, dotted, and as a DNS answer, were fetched by all three languages because the 6to4 rule returned before the ISATAP rule ran; the reference also refused every dotted-tail IPv6 literal, even a public one, which url-0023 pins as a control. Every column was observed by executing each language's guarded fetch. Corpus 0.1.44 adds url-0024 to url-0039 (G-386), the first WIRE rows (`transport: "default"`): a host spelled so that a guard and its HTTP client could read it differently -- percent escapes, a backslash, inet_aton numeric forms, full-width and other non-ASCII spellings -- fetched over each language's REAL default client against a loopback server, with a resolver that answers public for every spelling (and the truth for `localhost`). `dispatched` is read off the server, which is the only place a guard-versus-client differential shows: the per-language runners stub the client and record what the guard decided. Against the code before G-382, PHP (prism 524baf6, and f5092b8 after #185) CONNECTED to loopback on all five numeric rows and on the Latin-1 superscript row over Guzzle 8.6, and prism-py b906a80 CONNECTED on the three percent-escaped rows; on current main nothing reaches the server in any language. The non-ASCII rows disagree by design and are recorded: PHP refuses a host outside printable ASCII and TypeScript judges the folded WHATWG host, while Python resolves the written name and pins its connection to the vetted answer, so it records no refusal code and reaches nothing.

discrimination.note: url-0001 fetches successfully and distinguishes a guard that refuses everything. url-0009 preserves the existing unguarded loopback path in PHP and TypeScript; Python has no such path. url-0039 runs the UNGUARDED fetch against the same loopback server and is dispatched in PHP and TypeScript, so a `dispatched: false` on a wire row is a measurement, not a dead socket; url-0037 (localhost, answered honestly) and url-0038 (the canonical literal) are the refused baselines.

php.note: Wire rows (`transport: "default"`) are run by prism-parity:tools/media-fetch-guard.mjs php --check against the default branch, and skipped by the in-repository runner.

ts.note: Wire rows (`transport: "default"`) are run by prism-parity:tools/media-fetch-guard.mjs ts --check against the default branch, and skipped by the in-repository runner.

py.note: url-0009 is explicitly skipped for py: no unguarded media fetch exists by design. Wire rows (`transport: "default"`) are run by prism-parity:tools/media-fetch-guard.mjs py --check against the default branch, and skipped by the in-repository runner.
